Your agent can learn a database it has never seen, prepare a schema change
against it, and follow that change until it finishes. SchemaBot gives it what
it needs: a live schema to read, a plan to check before anything runs, and
JSON output to parse.

The first half of this page covers what to give your agent so it can do that
work well. The second half covers the decisions that stay with you.

<a id="install-the-schemabot-agent-skill"></a>

## Install the agent skill

[`skills/schemabot`](../skills/schemabot/SKILL.md) is a ready-made agent skill,
and the quickest way to get started. It teaches your agent to edit schema
files, read a plan, take a pull request through each environment, and clear a
check that is stuck waiting.

The skill's [command policy](../skills/schemabot/references/command-policy.md)
lists every PR comment command and says whether your agent posts it, asks you
first, or hands it to you to post. The policy is the complete list. This page
explains the reasoning behind it.

The skill is a standard `SKILL.md` directory in the
[Agent Skills](https://agentskills.io) format, which Claude Code, Codex,
goose, and other agents load. Copy the directory to wherever your agent loads
skills from. For Claude Code, that is `.claude/skills/` in your repository or
`~/.claude/skills/`; other agents document their own location.

Copy the skill from a release tag rather than from `main`. That way it matches
the SchemaBot version you run, and changes on `main` reach your agent only when
you upgrade.

CI checks every `schemabot` command in the skill against the PR comment parser
and the CLI. An example that SchemaBot would reject fails the build.

## What your agent can do

### Learn a database

Your agent does not need you to describe your schema. It can look it up.

| Question | Command |
|---|---|
| Which databases are there, and on which engines and environments? | `databases` |
| What is in this database right now? | `pull` returns the live schema as SQL or JSON. `onboard` writes it to a new schema directory |
| What is running right now? | `status` lists the active applies, followed by recent finished ones. `locks` shows which databases are locked |
| What has run against this database? | `status -d <database>` lists its past applies. `status <apply_id>` and `logs <apply_id>` show one in detail |
| What changes have been planned for it? | `list-plans` lists stored plans, whether or not they were applied |

[Schema intelligence](schema-intelligence.md) walks through each of these,
including structured columns and indexes, lint findings on the live schema,
and databases with several targets. The same answers are available over HTTP,
so an agent without a shell can use them too.

### Prepare a change

Your agent edits the `CREATE TABLE` files to describe the schema you want. It
does not write `ALTER` statements or numbered change scripts; SchemaBot works
out the DDL.

`plan` shows the exact DDL SchemaBot would run, with any lint findings, before
anything touches the database. Your agent can read what the change will do,
and so can you.

Creating a plan takes write access. A read-only agent can find the same DDL in
the plan comment SchemaBot posts on the pull request, or in a stored plan from
`list-plans`.

### Follow a change

While a change runs, `status` gives its current state, `progress --no-watch`
shows how far along it is, and `logs` shows its log.

Have your agent pass `--no-watch`. Without it, `progress` opens an interactive
watcher, and its keys can stop or cancel the change, run its cutover, or close
its revert window.

When a change runs on several targets or shards, progress shows each one
separately, so your agent can tell you which one is behind. To read the log of
just one, use `logs --target` or `logs --shard`; see
[Read the logs](cli.md#read-the-logs).

### Read the output as JSON

These commands can return JSON, so your agent does not have to parse output
formatted for a terminal.

| Commands | JSON option |
|---|---|
| `databases`, `status`, `progress`, `list-plans`, `logs`, `locks`, `plan`, `init`, `settings`, `freeze list`, `freeze show`, `freeze override`, `checks show` | `--json` |
| `pull` | `-o json` |

`apply -o json` streams progress as the change runs rather than returning a
single JSON document. `progress --json` prints one snapshot and never opens
the interactive watcher.

For more output options, see
[Use the CLI from scripts and agents](cli.md#use-the-cli-from-scripts-and-agents).
For the same reads over HTTP, see the
[schema intelligence guide](schema-intelligence.md).

## Give it its own account

Which account your agent uses decides whose name goes on its work.

- **With its own account**, give it read-only access to inspect schemas and
  follow changes. The [authentication guide](auth.md#calling-schemabot-as-a-service)
  explains how to set this up. This is the better choice: its reads are
  recorded as its own, and it cannot change anything, even by mistake.
- **With your account**, its actions are recorded as yours. If it runs the CLI
  with your credentials or posts a comment from your GitHub account, SchemaBot
  cannot tell whether you or your agent sent the command.

The guidance below is a cautious starting point you can adapt for your team.
The agent skill already follows it. It also covers the rules you can add for
your team and the settings you can enforce on the server.

## You decide what runs in production

Let your agent prepare the change and explain what will happen. Under the
policy below, you run the production command yourself. The final decision
stays with you, and the record shows who actually took it.

PR approval is a separate check. Where the review gate is enabled, SchemaBot
requires approval before applying a change. The check still applies when
your agent sends the command, but SchemaBot cannot tell whether you reviewed
what your agent is about to do with your credentials.

## Decide when your agent should ask

| Task | Suggested boundary |
|---|---|
| Run a production command such as `apply`, `apply-confirm`, `cutover`, or `rollback` | You run it yourself, even if you asked your agent to |
| Run a command with `--allow-unsafe`, `--skip-revert`, or `--force`, in any environment | You review what it gives up and run the command yourself |
| Ask to override a freeze with `--override`, in any environment | You decide whether to ask, write the reason, and run the command yourself. See [guidance for agents](freeze.md#guidance-for-agents) |
| Apply to a shared staging database or one that other teams depend on | Your agent hands you the command |
| Apply to a new or isolated staging database with little impact on others | Your agent explains what it will do, then proceeds |
| Apply when it is unclear who depends on the database | Your agent hands you the command |
| Outside production, run `apply-confirm`, `release`, `unlock`, `rollback`, `revert`, or `skip-revert` | Your agent says what the command will do and asks first |
| Inspect status, progress, history, a stored plan, or the live schema | Your agent can use its read access without asking each time |

If you prefer to run every write command yourself, say so in your agent's
instructions. That takes precedence over the staging defaults above.

Staging changes can affect other people too. A change can disrupt their tests
or hold a database lock while it runs. Use your team's service criticality
ratings if you have them; otherwise, treat any staging database you cannot
confirm is isolated as shared. Any configured approval requirements still apply.

<a id="give-your-agent-clear-instructions"></a>

## Add your own rules

The [agent skill](#install-the-agent-skill) already gives your agent every
rule on this page, so there is nothing to copy. Your own instructions only
need what differs for you. For example:

- You run every write command yourself, in every environment.
- A staging database counts as shared, whatever its criticality rating says.

## Back it up with server settings

Instructions guide your agent. Server settings control what it can do with
the credentials you give it. They cannot make an action “human only” when
the agent uses your credentials.

- **Give services their own read-only access.** With a service mesh,
  `forward_auth` can limit requests from listed services to reads. With OIDC,
  keep admin and operator groups out of service tokens. A token with either
  group can write, even when it belongs to a service. See
  [service access](auth.md#calling-schemabot-as-a-service).
- **Choose which accounts can run PR commands.** Enable
  `pr_command_authorization`. To keep a bot account read-only, leave it out of
  the admin and operator grants, including repository-level admin grants. See
  [GitHub permissions](auth.md#github-side-authorization).
- **Require review before apply.** Enable
  [`review_policy`](configuration.md#review-gate) on the server to require an
  approval for every database it serves, or on one database to require it
  there alone. The PR author's own approval does not count. By default, an
  approval keeps counting after later pushes until the reviewer requests
  changes or GitHub dismisses it. To require a fresh approval whenever the
  schema change differs from the approved one, set `require_reapproval: true`.
- **Review destructive changes before allowing them.** Changes flagged as unsafe
  require `--allow-unsafe` to proceed. If your agent uses your credentials, it
  can pass that flag too, and SchemaBot cannot tell whether you approved the
  change yourself.
- **Check the logs when a command is denied.** They say why it was blocked,
  which helps you check the caller's permissions. The
  `schemabot.pr_command_actor_authorization.total` metric shows patterns
  across many requests.
